subject: Renal
vignette: A 24-year-old man has a routine physical examination. Serum glucose is 85 mg/dL and urinalysis shows no glucose. His proximal tubules are functioning normally.
question: Which mechanism is primarily responsible for the absence of glucose in this patient's urine at a normal plasma glucose concentration?

options.text: Passive diffusion of glucose across the thin descending limb
Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransport in the thick ascending limb
Glucose secretion into the tubular lumen by the distal convoluted tubule
Na+/glucose cotransport in the proximal convoluted tubule
Aldosterone-driven ENaC reabsorption in the collecting duct

explanation_correct: At plasma glucose of 60-120 mg/dL, essentially all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule by sodium-glucose cotransport at the brush border, so no glucose appears in urine. This saturable, carrier-mediated process reaches its maximum (Tm approximately 375 mg/min) only at much higher glucose levels. The renal threshold (~200 mg/dL) is the plasma level at which glucosuria first appears.

explanation_incorrect.A: The thin descending limb is permeable mainly to water, not glucose; it concentrates urine and does not reabsorb glucose.
explanation_incorrect.B: The Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter is in the thick ascending limb and handles salts, not glucose; it is the loop diuretic target.
explanation_incorrect.C: Glucose is not secreted in the distal tubule; under normal conditions it is completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.
explanation_incorrect.E: ENaC in the collecting duct reabsorbs sodium under aldosterone control and is not involved in glucose handling.

educationalObjective: Normal plasma glucose is completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule via Na+/glucose cotransport, so urine is glucose-free.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has a plasma glucose of 220 mg/dL. A urine sample tests positive for glucose. His GFR is normal at 100 mL/min.
question: The appearance of glucose in the urine at this plasma concentration reflects which renal concept?

options.text: The tubular maximum (Tm) for glucose has been reached at this plasma level
The renal threshold for glucose (~200 mg/dL) has been exceeded
Complete saturation of all sodium-glucose transporters
A reduction in GFR below normal
Increased glucose secretion by the proximal tubule

explanation_correct: Glucosuria begins at a plasma glucose of about 200 mg/dL, the renal threshold, which is well below the plasma level needed to saturate all transporters (Tm approximately 375 mg/min). At 220 mg/dL, the filtered glucose load exceeds the reabsorptive capacity of some nephrons, so glucose spills into urine. Complete saturation (Tm) occurs only at much higher glucose levels.

explanation_incorrect.A: Tm (~375 mg/min) is reached at a much higher plasma glucose than 220 mg/dL; the threshold is crossed first.
explanation_incorrect.C: Not all transporters are saturated at 220 mg/dL; some reabsorption continues, which is why excretion rises gradually (splay).
explanation_incorrect.D: GFR is normal here; glucosuria at this level reflects a filtered load exceeding reabsorptive capacity, not reduced filtration.
explanation_incorrect.E: Glucose is not secreted by the proximal tubule; glucosuria results from incomplete reabsorption, not secretion.

educationalObjective: Glucosuria begins at the renal threshold (~200 mg/dL), before the tubular maximum (Tm ~375 mg/min) is reached.

subject: Renal
vignette: A physiology student examines a glucose titration curve: excreted glucose rises gradually between plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL and the point of maximal reabsorption, rather than jumping abruptly from zero to maximal excretion.
question: Which explanation best accounts for this gradual rise (the splay phenomenon)?

options.text: GFR progressively rises as plasma glucose increases
Glucose is increasingly secreted by the distal nephron at high plasma levels
Nephron heterogeneity: individual nephrons have different transport maxima (Tm)
Aldosterone activity increases glucose reabsorption in the collecting duct
The glomerular charge barrier becomes saturated with glucose

explanation_correct: The splay phenomenon is the gradual increase in glucose excretion between the threshold and the Tm, caused by nephron heterogeneity: different nephrons have different Tm values and reach saturation at different plasma glucose levels. As a result, some nephrons spill glucose while others still reabsorb it, producing a smooth curve rather than a sharp corner. GFR is constant and glucose is not secreted.

explanation_incorrect.A: GFR is essentially constant over this range; the splay reflects varying nephron Tm, not changing filtration.
explanation_incorrect.B: Glucose is reabsorbed, not secreted, in the proximal tubule; there is no distal glucose secretion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Aldosterone regulates sodium, potassium, and hydrogen handling in the collecting duct, not glucose reabsorption.
explanation_incorrect.E: Glucose is freely filtered and not charge-restricted; the charge barrier concerns proteins such as albumin.

educationalObjective: Splay is the gradual rise in glucosuria between threshold and Tm caused by nephron heterogeneity in glucose transport maxima.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 28-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation has a fasting serum glucose of 92 mg/dL, yet a routine urinalysis shows 2+ glucose. She has no history of diabetes and her HbA1c is normal.
question: Which change in renal physiology best explains glucosuria at a normal plasma glucose concentration in this patient?

options.text: Increased proximal tubular Na+/glucose cotransporter density raising the Tm
Decreased GFR reducing the filtered glucose load
Gain-of-function mutation in the glucose transporter causing over-reabsorption
Increased aldosterone driving glucose secretion in the collecting duct
Increased GFR lowering the plasma glucose threshold

explanation_correct: Normal pregnancy is associated with an increased GFR, so more glucose is filtered at any given plasma concentration. Because the filtered load rises, the renal threshold is reached at a lower plasma glucose, producing glucosuria despite normal serum glucose; this is physiologic and not diagnostic of diabetes. The Tm is not raised; rather the threshold shifts downward.

explanation_incorrect.A: Increasing transporter density/Tm would reduce glucosuria, not cause it; pregnancy does not raise the Tm.
explanation_incorrect.B: GFR is increased, not decreased, in pregnancy; a lower GFR would lower the filtered load and reduce glucosuria.
explanation_incorrect.C: A gain-of-function transporter would enhance reabsorption and prevent glucose loss; pregnancy does not involve such a mutation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Aldosterone does not regulate glucose transport; glucosuria here is due to the increased filtered load.

educationalObjective: Pregnancy raises GFR, lowering the glucose threshold so glucosuria can occur at normal plasma glucose.
source: Generated from 14. Renal.pdf - Physiology: Glucose clearance, threshold, and splay

subject: Renal
vignette: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes starts empagliflozin. He develops glycosuria while his serum glucose is 150 mg/dL, well below the usual threshold of about 200 mg/dL.
question: Which statement best explains this drug-induced glucosuria?

options.text: SGLT2 inhibition reduces proximal glucose reabsorption, causing glucosuria below the usual threshold
The drug raises the renal threshold for glucose above 200 mg/dL
The drug increases the tubular maximum (Tm) for glucose reabsorption
The drug causes glucose secretion in the distal convoluted tubule
The drug reduces GFR so filtered glucose exceeds reabsorptive capacity

explanation_correct: SGLT2 inhibitors (the -flozin drugs) block the sodium-glucose cotransporter in the proximal tubule, reducing glucose reabsorption so glucose is excreted at plasma concentrations below 200 mg/dL. This glucosuria occurs at lower plasma glucose than the normal renal threshold and is a clinical clue to the drug's mechanism. The effective Tm is reduced, not raised, and GFR is not the primary driver.

explanation_incorrect.B: The drug lowers the effective threshold for glucose spillage; it does not raise it above 200 mg/dL.
explanation_incorrect.C: Inhibiting the transporter reduces the tubular maximum for reabsorption rather than increasing it.
explanation_incorrect.D: The drug blocks reabsorption in the proximal tubule; it does not stimulate distal glucose secretion.
explanation_incorrect.E: SGLT2 inhibitors do not lower GFR as their primary glucosuric mechanism; the effect is reduced proximal reabsorption.

educationalObjective: SGLT2 (-flozin) inhibitors cause glucosuria at plasma glucose <200 mg/dL by blocking proximal tubular glucose reabsorption.
